## STEP 1 — GATHER REAL DATA (mandatory)

You MUST use your web search and shell tools to visit authoritative sources and extract real data.
Do NOT skip this step. Do NOT rely on memory alone — actually search and read real pages.

   latest scientific opinion or re-evaluation. Extract: approval status, ADI (value + unit),
   evaluation year, key conclusions.

2. **FDA/CFR**: Search ecfr.gov for the additive name in Title 21 (Food and Drugs).
   Extract: GRAS status, specific CFR section citation, any conditions of use.

3. **JECFA/WHO**: Search apps.who.int/food-additives-contaminants-jecfa-database/
   or who.int for the additive. Extract: ADI, last evaluation year.

4. **IARC**: Check monographs.iarc.who.int for any classification.

5. **PubMed**: Search pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov for recent safety studies on this additive.

For each source, record the actual URL you visited and the specific data you found.
If a page is inaccessible, note that and try alternative search queries.

File 1: /home/exedev/chewber/research/additives/E102/E102-report.md

  - **Identity**: E-number, CAS number(s), chemical class, common synonyms, natural vs synthetic
  - **Function in Food**: mechanism of action, common food categories
  - **Regulatory Status**: EFSA opinion + ADI, FDA GRAS + CFR citation, JECFA ADI, IARC, notable bans
  - **Key Safety Evidence**: animal studies, epidemiological data, mechanistic concerns
  - **Exposure Assessment**: typical dietary intake, ADI exceedance risk, vulnerable populations
  - **Risk Assessment**: recommend a Chewber tier with rationale:

3150:<P><I>Accreditation</I> means a determination by a recognized accreditation body (or, in the case of direct accreditation, by FDA) that a third-party certification body meets the applicable requirements of this subpart.
3152:<P><I>Accreditation body</I> means an authority that performs accreditation of third-party certification bodies.
3154:<P><I>Accredited third-party certification body</I> means a third-party certification body that a recognized accreditation body (or, in the case of direct accreditation, FDA) has determined meets the applicable requirements of this subpart and is accredited to conduct food safety audits and to issue food or facility certifications to eligible entities. An accredited third-party certification body has the same meaning as accredited third-party auditor as defined in section 808(a)(4) of the FD&amp;C Act.
3160:<P>(ii) With respect to a third-party certification body, an evaluation by a recognized accreditation body (or, in the case of direct accreditation, FDA) of the competency and capacity of a third-party certification body under the applicable requirements of this subpart for the defined scope of accreditation. An assessment of the competency and capacity of the third-party certification body involves evaluating the competency and capacity of the operations of the third-party certification body that are relevant to decisions on accreditation and, if accredited, an evaluation of its performance and the validity of its audit results and certification decisions under the applicable requirements of this subpart.
3162:<P><I>Audit</I> means the systematic and functionally independent examination of an eligible entity under this subpart by an accredited third-party certification body or by FDA. An audit conducted under this subpart is not considered an inspection under section 704 of the FD&amp;C Act.
3164:<P><I>Audit agent</I> means an individual who is an employee or other agent of an accredited third-party certification body who, although not individually accredited, is qualified to conduct food safety audits on behalf of an accredited third-party certification body. An audit agent includes a contractor of the accredited third-party certification body but excludes subcontractors or other agents under outsourcing arrangements for conducting food safety audits without direct control by the accredited third-party certification body.
3172:<P>(iii) That is conducted in preparation for a regulatory audit; only the results of a regulatory audit may form the basis for issuance of a food or facility certification under this subpart.
3174:<P><I>Direct accreditation</I> means accreditation of a third-party certification body by FDA.
3176:<P><I>Eligible entity</I> means a foreign entity in the import supply chain of food for consumption in the United States that chooses to be subject to a food safety audit under this subpart conducted by an accredited third-party certification body. Eligible entities include foreign facilities required to be registered under subpart H of this part.
3180:<P><I>Facility certification</I> means an attestation, issued for purposes of section 801(q) or 806 of the FD&amp;C Act by an accredited third-party certification body, after conducting a regulatory audit and any other activities necessary to establish whether a facility complies with the applicable food safety requirements of the FD&amp;C Act and FDA regulations.
3184:<P><I>Food certification</I> means an attestation, issued for purposes of section 801(q) of the FD&amp;C Act by an accredited third-party certification body, after conducting a regulatory audit and any other activities necessary to establish whether a food of an eligible entity complies with the applicable food safety requirements of the FD&amp;C Act and FDA regulations.
3190:<P><I>Recognized accreditation body</I> means an accreditation body that FDA has determined meets the applicable requirements of this subpart and is authorized to accredit third-party certification bodies under this subpart.
3196:<P>(ii) The results of which are used in determining eligibility for certification under section 801(q) or under section 806 of the FD&amp;C Act.
3200:<P>(i) With respect to an accreditation body, a decision to cede voluntarily its authority to accredit third-party certification bodies as a recognized accreditation body prior to expiration of its recognition under this subpart; and
3202:<P>(ii) With respect to a third-party certification body, a decision to cede voluntarily its authority to conduct food safety audits and to issue food and facility certifications to eligible entities as an accredited third-party certification body prior to expiration of its accreditation under this subpart.

33186:<P>(2) The label of OTC and prescription drug products intended for human use administered orally, nasally, rectally, or vaginally, or for use in the area of the eye, containing FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 shall specifically declare the presence of FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 by listing the color additive using the names FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 and tartrazine. The label shall bear a statement such as “Contains FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) as a color additive” or “Contains color additives including FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine).” The labels of certain drug products subject to this labeling requirement that are also cosmetics, such as: antibacterial mouthwashes and fluoride toothpastes, need not comply with this requirement provided they comply with the requirements of § 701.3 of this chapter.
33188:<P>(3) For prescription drugs for human use containing FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 that are administered orally, nasally, vaginally, or rectally, or for use in the area of the eye, the labeling required by § 201.100(d) of this chapter shall, in addition to the label statement required under paragraph (c)(2) of this section, bear the warning statement “This product contains FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) which may cause allergic-type reactions (including bronchial asthma) in certain susceptible persons. Although the overall incidence of FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) sensitivity in the general population is low, it is frequently seen in patients who also have aspirin hypersensitivity.” This warning statement shall appear in the “Precautions” section of the labeling.
113028:<P>(a) The label for over-the-counter and prescription drug products intended for human use administered orally, nasally, rectally, or vaginally, or for use in the area of the eye, containing FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 as a color additive using the names FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 and tartrazine. The labeling for over-the-counter and prescription drug products shall bear a statement such as “Contains FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) as a color additive” or “Contains color additives including FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine)”. The labels of certain drug products subject to this labeling requirement that are also cosmetics, such as antibacterial mouthwashes and fluoride toothpastes, need not comply with this requirement provided they comply with the requirements of § 701.3 of this chapter.
113030:<P>(b) For prescription drugs for human use containing FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 that are administered orally, nasally, vaginally, or rectally, or for use in the area of the eye, the labeling required by § 201.100(d) shall bear the warning statement “This product contains FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) which may cause allergic-type reactions (including bronchial asthma) in certain susceptible persons. Although the overall incidence of FD&amp;C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) sensitivity in the general population is low, it is frequently seen in patients who also have aspirin hypersensitivity.” This warning statement shall appear in the “Precautions” section of the labeling.

# E102 (Tartrazine) Research Report

## Identity
- **E-number:** E102
- **Name:** Tartrazine
- **CAS number(s):** 1934-21-0
- **Chemical class:** Synthetic azo dye (sulfonated monoazo food color)
- **Common synonyms:** FD&C Yellow No. 5, INS 102, C.I. Food Yellow 4, Acid Yellow 23
- **Origin:** Synthetic

**Evidence:**
- 21 CFR §74.705 identifies FD&C Yellow No. 5 and gives CAS 1934-21-0 plus synthetic manufacturing route ([S3], [S4]).
- WHO/JECFA entry is for TARTRAZINE with ADI listing ([S6]).

## Function in Food
- **Primary function:** Color additive (yellow coloring agent).
- **Mechanism of action in foods:** The azo chromophore absorbs visible light and imparts a yellow hue; used to standardize/restore product color.
- **Common food categories:** Beverages, confectionery, desserts, snacks, sauces/condiments, and dietary supplements.

**Evidence:**
- FDA allows FD&C Yellow No. 5 for coloring foods generally under GMP (with restrictions) ([S4]).

## Regulatory Status
### EFSA (EU)
- **Latest EFSA re-evaluation located:** 2009 Scientific Opinion, \"Scientific Opinion on the re-evaluation Tartrazine (E 102)\" ([S1], [S2]).
- **Status:** Approved (re-evaluated; ADI retained).
- **ADI:** 7.5 mg/kg bw/day.
- **Key EFSA conclusion:** Available toxicology database was considered more extensive than previous evaluations; no reason to revise the ADI; impurity exposure at current specs was not considered a safety concern.

**Access note:** direct EFSA/Wiley opinion page was not machine-accessible from this environment (bot challenge/403); data above were taken from EFSA result metadata/snippet and EFSA DOI metadata pages that were accessible ([S1], [S2]).

### FDA / eCFR (United States)
- **Status:** Approved color additive, **not GRAS-listed**.
- **Primary citation:** **21 CFR §74.705** (FD&C Yellow No. 5) ([S3], [S4]).
- **Conditions of use (foods):** \"may be safely used for coloring foods (including dietary supplements) generally\" under GMP, with standard-of-identity restrictions; labeling declaration required; batch certification required ([S4]).
- **GRAS inference:** Tartrazine appears as a certified color additive in Part 74 and was not found as a GRAS substance by additive name in Title 21 text extraction. This is an inference from the eCFR structure/search results, not a single explicit \"not GRAS\" sentence ([S4]).

### JECFA / WHO
- **Entry:** TARTRAZINE, JECFA database chemical page ([S6]).
- **Latest evaluation year:** 2016.
- **ADI:** 0-10 mg/kg bw.
- **Key conclusion:** JECFA established ADI 0-10 mg/kg bw (NOAEL 984 mg/kg bw/day, UF 100), withdrew previous ADI 0-7.5 mg/kg bw/day, and stated estimated dietary exposure (including children 1-10 years) was below the upper ADI bound ([S6]).

### IARC
- **Finding from IARC Monographs classification resources:** No tartrazine entry found in the current \"List of Classifications\" dataset (updated 2026-02-25 in the served script) ([S7], [S8], [S9]).
- **Interpretation:** No current IARC group classification could be confirmed from the live IARC classification dataset accessed.

### Notable bans
- No current major-jurisdiction ban was confirmed in the sources collected for this run.

## Key Safety Evidence
### Animal and mechanistic evidence
- Multiple recent animal studies report oxidative stress, histopathology, or neurobehavioral changes with tartrazine exposure, often at high dose and/or short-to-medium study duration (e.g., pancreatic and brain injury models) ([S12], [S13], [S14]).
- A 2026 OECD/AOP-oriented paper reported endocrine-activity signals primarily from in silico/in vitro integration, indicating hypothesis-generating concern rather than definitive clinical risk quantification ([S11]).

### Human/epidemiological evidence
- The 2007 Southampton randomized trial found increased hyperactivity scores with **mixtures** of artificial colors plus sodium benzoate in children; causality for tartrazine alone is not isolated ([S15]).
- A 2022 review (OEHHA-linked) found many challenge studies indicating behavioral associations for synthetic food dyes and highlighted concern for susceptible children ([S10]).

### Allergic/hypersensitivity concern
- U.S. labeling rules include explicit warning language for FD&C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) sensitivity in certain susceptible persons, including bronchial-asthma-type reactions and higher prevalence among aspirin-hypersensitive patients (drug-label context in Title 21 text) ([S4]).

## Exposure Assessment
- **JECFA (2016):** exposure estimates for general population, including children 1-10 years, were reported below the upper ADI bound ([S6]).
- **ADI exceedance risk:** not clearly demonstrated in the regulatory sources collected here for the general population; high-intake subgroups remain a practical concern in principle.
- **Vulnerable populations:**
  - Children with high intake of dyed foods/beverages.
  - Individuals with aspirin hypersensitivity or known dye sensitivity.

## Risk Assessment (Chewber Tier)
- **Recommended tier:** "'`moderate`
- **Rationale:** Tartrazine is approved by EFSA/FDA/JECFA with established ADIs and certification controls, but there are persistent caveats: behavioral signal literature (especially in children for synthetic dye mixtures), repeated animal/mechanistic toxicity findings, and known hypersensitivity labeling concerns. Carcinogenic classification evidence from IARC was not confirmed as positive in current accessed data.
- **Confidence:** Moderate (source quality is mixed across regulatory and experimental evidence; EFSA full opinion text was not directly retrievable in this environment).

## Sources
- **[S1]** EFSA Journal page: *Scientific Opinion on the re-evaluation Tartrazine (E 102)* (2009). URL: https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/efsajournal/pub/1331 (redirects to Wiley in current deployment).
- **[S2]** Crossref metadata for DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2009.1331 (2009 metadata record). URL: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2903/j.efsa.2009.1331
- **[S3]** eCFR section URL for FD&C Yellow No. 5. URL: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-74/subpart-A/section-74.705
- **[S4]** eCFR API full XML, Title 21 (issue date 2026-02-19), containing §74.705 text and related labeling references. URL: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-02-19/title-21.xml
- **[S5]** eCFR titles endpoint (latest issue date context for Title 21). URL: https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/titles.json
- **[S6]** WHO/JECFA chemical page: TARTRAZINE (ID 3885), including ADI and evaluation year. URL: https://apps.who.int/food-additives-contaminants-jecfa-database/Home/Chemical/3885
- **[S7]** IARC classifications landing page. URL: https://monographs.iarc.who.int/agents-classified-by-the-iarc/
- **[S8]** IARC "List of classifications" page. URL: https://monographs.iarc.who.int/list-of-classifications/
- **[S9]** IARC list data script (contains current classification dataset and update timestamp). URL: https://webapi.iarc.who.int/loc/loc.app.js
- **[S10]** Miller et al., *Potential impacts of synthetic food dyes on activity and attention in children* (Environ Health, 2022). URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35484553/
- **[S11]** Hoang & Park, *Integrated approaches to testing and assessment for the endocrine disrupting activity of tartrazine* (Food Chem Toxicol, 2026). URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41297657/
- **[S12]** Rodrigues et al., *Cognitive and Behavioral Effects of Chronic Tartrazine Use in vivo* (J Mol Neurosci, 2025). URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40968326/
- **[S13]** Vaithilingam et al., *Chronic exposure to food additives... gut-brain axis in zebrafish* (Sci Total Environ, 2025). URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40848430/
- **[S14]** Erdemli et al., *Protective effects of thymoquinone against tartrazine-induced pancreatic injury* (Arch Physiol Biochem, 2026). URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40638124/
- **[S15]** McCann et al., *Food additives and hyperactive behaviour...* (Lancet, 2007). URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17825405/
EOF
